hints: Think about what a wave model would predict - if light were only a continuous wave spreading energy, how should brighter light and waiting longer affect electrons?
Focus on how the observations split into two separate roles - what controls how energetic each electron is, compared with what controls how many electrons come out per second?
Remember the two most surprising timing and frequency clues - is there a cut-off frequency, and is there any delay before emission starts?
walkthrough:
**Why Wave Theory Fails**
Think of light as a wave spreading energy continuously. Brighter light should give more energetic electrons, any frequency should eventually work if you wait long enough, and there should be a time delay while energy builds up. None of this is observed, so we need particles.

**Energy Comes in Packets**
In the photon picture, one photon hits one electron in a one-to-one interaction with energy $$E = hf$$. So the maximum energy of the emitted electron depends on frequency $f$, not on intensity. Increasing intensity only increases the number of photons, so it increases the rate of emission, not the energy of each electron.

**Threshold and Instant Action**
If $$hf$$ is less than the work function $\Phi$, no electron can escape, giving a threshold frequency $f_0$ below which there is zero emission whatever the intensity. Since energy arrives in a concentrated packet, absorption is instantaneous with no delay.

Final answer: Any three from: max KE of electrons depends on frequency, not intensity; rate of emission depends on intensity at constant frequency; threshold frequency below which no emission; instantaneous emission with no time delay.

hints: Start by thinking about what determines the energy of a single packet of light - which two universal constants link that energy to the given wavelength?
Use $$E = hc/\lambda$$ with $\lambda = 380 \text{ nm} = 380 \times 10^{-9} \text{ m}$ to find $E$ in joules.
Convert your joule answer to electronvolts by dividing by $1.60 \times 10^{-19} \text{ J eV}^{-1}$ and give 2 or 3 s.f.
walkthrough:
**Photon Energy From Wavelength**
A photon of frequency $f$ and wavelength $\lambda$ carries energy $$E = hf = \frac{hc}{\lambda}$$ where $h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34} \text{ J s}$ and $c = 3.0 \times 10^{8} \text{ m s}^{-1}$.

**Calculate in Joules**
Convert wavelength to metres: $$\lambda = 380 \text{ nm} = 380 \times 10^{-9} \text{ m}$$ Then $$E = \frac{(6.63 \times 10^{-34})(3.0 \times 10^{8})}{380 \times 10^{-9}}$$ $$E = 5.23 \times 10^{-19} \text{ J}$$

**Convert to Electronvolts**
Since $1 \text{ eV} = 1.60 \times 10^{-19} \text{ J}$: $$E = \frac{5.23 \times 10^{-19}}{1.60 \times 10^{-19}}$$ $$E = 3.3 \text{ eV}$$ to 2 s.f.

hints: Think about the energy budget for one electron - how does the incoming photon energy compare with the minimum energy needed to escape the metal?
Compare your 3.3 eV photon to each work function in Fig. 11.1 and pick out where the photon has a surplus.
walkthrough:
**Condition for Emission**
From $$hf = \Phi + K_{max}$$, an electron can only escape if the photon supplies at least the work function: $$hf > \Phi$$ If the photon energy is smaller than $\Phi$, no photoelectrons are released.

**Apply to the Table**
Photon energy is $3.3 \text{ eV}$. Sodium $\Phi = 2.4 \text{ eV} < 3.3 \text{ eV}$ - yes. Calcium $\Phi = 2.9 \text{ eV} < 3.3 \text{ eV}$ - yes. Zinc $3.6 \text{ eV}$ and silver $4.3 \text{ eV}$ are greater than $3.3 \text{ eV}$ - no emission. So sodium and calcium only.
Final answer: Emission requires photon energy > work function energy. $3.3 \text{ eV}$ exceeds 2.4 eV and 2.9 eV, so sodium and calcium emit photoelectrons.

hints: Think in terms of momentum, not energy - when a photon is absorbed, what happens to the momentum it was carrying and what does that mean for the surface?
Find the momentum of one photon using $$p = h/\lambda$$ with $\lambda = 380 \times 10^{-9} \text{ m}$.
Link total force to the arrival rate using force = rate of change of momentum = $p \times$ number per second.
walkthrough:
**Photons Carry Momentum**
Even though photons have no mass, they carry momentum $$p = \frac{h}{\lambda}$$ When absorbed normally, each photon gives all its momentum to the surface. Force is the total momentum delivered per second.

**Momentum of One Photon**
$$p = \frac{6.63 \times 10^{-34}}{380 \times 10^{-9}}$$ $$p = 1.74 \times 10^{-27} \text{ kg m s}^{-1} = 1.74 \times 10^{-27} \text{ N s}$$

**From Rate to Force**
With $N = 7.6 \times 10^{14} \text{ s}^{-1}$ photons absorbed per second: $$F = \frac{\Delta p}{\Delta t} = Np$$ $$F = (7.6 \times 10^{14})(1.74 \times 10^{-27})$$ $$F = 1.3 \times 10^{-12} \text{ N}$$ in the direction of the incident light.
Final answer: $p = 1.74 \times 10^{-27} \text{ N s}$, force $= p \times 7.6 \times 10^{14} = 1.3 \times 10^{-12} \text{ N}$.
